content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the shadow of death' (Hebrew tsalmaveth) is primarily understood as a symbol of the deepest darkness and gloom associated with mortal peril — the near presence or looming threat of death — through which the believer may pass without fear because God is present. In the Psalm 23 tradition it represents extreme danger, suffering, or the experience of dying itself, with the emphasis that it is only a 'shadow' (a threat that cannot ultimately harm those under God's protection). In the prophetic and New Testament usage (Isaiah 9:2; Matthew 4:16; Luke 1:79), it is extended to mean the spiritual darkness, hopelessness, and condition of humanity apart from God, which is dispelled by the light of Christ.", "primary_basis": ["Psalm 23:4 ('Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil')", "Isaiah 9:2 ('the people that walked in darkness... they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined')", "Matthew 4:16 (quoting Isaiah 9:2 and applying it to Christ's ministry)", "Luke 1:79 (Zechariah's Benedictus: 'to give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death')", "Job 3:5; 10:21-22; 12:22; 24:17; 34:22 (repeated poetic usage for deep gloom and the realm of the dead)", "Psalm 44:19; Psalm 107:10-14 (deliverance from darkness and the shadow of death)", "Jeremiah 2:6; 13:16; Amos 5:8 (deep darkness imagery)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Lexical/critical reading: the Hebrew word is better vocalized tsalmut, meaning simply 'deep darkness' or 'thick gloom' (from a root meaning 'to be dark'), with no etymological connection to death. This underlies modern translations such as the NRSV's 'the darkest valley' in Psalm 23:4. On this reading the term symbolizes extreme darkness and danger generally rather than death specifically.", "basis": ["Modern lexicons (BDB, HALOT) and critical commentaries on Psalm 23:4 and Job", "Translation choices in NRSV, NIV footnotes, CEB, and other modern versions"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The shadow of death as spiritual death and the darkness of sin: humanity's fallen, unenlightened state prior to redemption, dispelled by Christ the light of the world. This is the dominant reading of the Isaiah 9:2 / Matthew 4:16 / Luke 1:79 strand and is prominent in patristic and homiletical tradition (e.g., readings connecting it to Gentile darkness or to the pre-Christian condition).", "basis": ["Matthew 4:16", "Luke 1:79", "Isaiah 9:2", "Patristic commentary (e.g., Augustine, Chrysostom) and later homiletical tradition"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The shadow of death as Sheol or the realm/land of the dead itself — a quasi-locative reading in which the phrase names the dark domain of the departed rather than a threat experienced by the living.", "basis": ["Job 10:21-22 ('the land of darkness and the shadow of death')", "Job 38:17 ('the gates of the shadow of death')"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The shadow of death as the experience of dying or the deathbed specifically — a devotional/pastoral reading of Psalm 23:4 in which the valley is the believer's own final passage from life to death, common in funeral liturgy and hymnody.", "basis": ["Psalm 23:4 as used in funeral rites, hymns, and devotional literature", "Puritan and later devotional writers (e.g., Bunyan's Valley of the Shadow of Death in Pilgrim's Progress, though Bunyan himself treats it as trials in life rather than dying)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "The shadow of death as depression, despair, or seasons of spiritual desolation in the believer's life — a modern pastoral-psychological application.", "basis": ["Contemporary pastoral and counseling literature applying Psalm 23:4", "Spurgeon and other preachers treating the valley as gloom and soul-trouble rather than literal death"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "There is a stable, recognizable consensus at the core: the phrase symbolizes the darkest, most death-threatening extremity of human experience, through which God accompanies and delivers his people, and — in the prophetic/NT strand — the darkness dispelled by Christ. The main live dispute is philological rather than theological: whether the Hebrew originally means 'shadow of death' (a compound with maveth, 'death') or simply 'deep darkness' (tsalmut). Even scholars who prefer 'deep darkness' generally acknowledge that the traditional 'shadow of death' reading, established by the Septuagint (skia thanatou) and the Vulgate, shaped the entire Christian interpretive tradition and the NT citations. The various readings (mortal peril, dying, Sheol, spiritual darkness, despair) are overlapping applications of the same core image rather than sharply competing symbol systems."}
